newsitem.title: ISRAEL: El Al chairman wants privatisation in two stages.
newsitem.headline: El Al chairman wants privatisation in two stages.

text.p: Shares in the Israeli state-owned carrier El Al Airlines should be floated in two stages rather than at once as the government is proposing, chairman Joseph Ciechanover said on Thursday.
Ciechanover said that if the government first sold only 51 percent of equity, it could sell the remaining 49 percent at a higher valuation later on.
"The privatisation of 51 percent will make El Al a non-governmental company and it will be able to do what it wants without (the interference of) the state," he said.

Ciechanover was referring to the ban on Sabbath flights imposed on El Al, which have hurt the carrier financially and caused underwriters to asssign it a very low valuation when the government considered floating shares in it last year.

A committee headed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's economic adviser, Moshe Leon, has proposed selling 100 percent of the airline sometime next year by issuing shares on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

At the time the panel cited a legal opinion that once the airline was no longer a state-owned enteprise it would not be required to adhere to the Sabbath prohibition. However, government sources have said that as long as the state holds shares in the airline, political pressures will probably dictate maintaining the ban.
Ciechanover said that all things being equal he expected the airline to turn profitable again in 1998 or 1999 after losing $80 million in 1996.
"Already in 1997 the loss will be considerably lower compared to the previous year," he said.
Last week El Al's board approved management's strategic plan which Ciechanover said calls among other things for dropping unprofitable routes.
"We haven't decided which routes yet, but are talking about three or four, including possibly the Tel Aviv-Delhi route," he said. "We will emphasise profitability and not market share."
The company will also increase capacity on profitable routes, like Tel Aviv-Hong Kong, and put special emphasis on customer service, he said.
